1780190881526.title: Chapter 1: A Tutorial Introduction
1780190881526.content:
Chapter 1: A Tutorial Introduction

In this chapter, we will walk through a series of simple C programs to show the essential elements of the language. Let's begin with the traditional first program: printing the message "hello, world". To run this in C, we must write a function named main, which is where program execution always begins. The library function printf is used to output text to the screen.

Here is the complete source code for the classic hello world program:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    printf("hello, world\n");
    return 0;
}

Let's examine this program in detail. The first line, #include <stdio.h>, tells the compiler to include information about the standard input/output library. The main function returns an integer value, which signals the success or failure of the program to the operating system. The statements of the function are enclosed in braces {}. The function printf is called with the argument "hello, world\n", where \n represents the newline character.

Next, let's look at variables and arithmetic expressions. The following program prints a table of Fahrenheit temperatures and their Celsius equivalents using the formula C = (5/9)(F-32):

#include <stdio.h>

/* print Fahrenheit-Celsius table
   for fahr = 0, 20, ..., 300 */
int main() {
    float fahr, celsius;
    float lower, upper, step;

    lower = 0;      /* lower limit of temperatuire table */
    upper = 300;    /* upper limit */
    step = 20;      /* step size */

    fahr = lower;
    while (fahr <= upper) {
        celsius = (5.0/9.0) * (fahr - 32.0);
        printf("%3.0f %6.1f\n", fahr, celsius);
        fahr = fahr + step;
    }
    return 0;
}

In C, all variables must be declared before they are used, usually at the beginning of the function before any executable statements. A declaration specifies a type, and contains a list of one or more variables of that type, such as int for integers and float for floating-point numbers. The while loop repeats as long as the condition in parentheses is true. The printf format string %3.0f specifies that a floating-point number is to be printed at least three characters wide, with no decimal point, while %6.1f specifies a number at least six characters wide, with one digit after the decimal point.

1780190881526.title: Chapter 2: Types, Operators and Expressions
1780190881526.content:
Chapter 2: Types, Operators and Expressions

Variables and constants are the basic data objects manipulated in a program. Declarations list the variables to be used, and state what type they have and perhaps what their initial values are. Operators specify what is to be done to them. Expressions combine variables and constants to produce new values. The type of an object determines what values it can have and what operations can be performed on it.

C provides only a few basic data types:

  • char: a single byte, capable of holding one character in the local character set.
  • int: an integer, typically reflecting the natural size of integers on the host machine.
  • float: single-precision floating point.
  • double: double-precision floating point.

In addition, there are a number of qualifiers that can be applied to these basic types. short and long apply to integers, allowing you to choose smaller or larger integer sizes as needed. The qualifiers signed or unsigned may be applied to char or any integer type, indicating whether the variable represents signed numbers or positive-only numbers respectively.

Let's write a utility function to compute the length of a string. In C, a string is represented as an array of characters ending with a null character '\0':

/* strlen: return length of s */
int strlen(char s[]) {
    int i = 0;
    while (s[i] != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
    return i;
}

Arithmetic operators include binary operators +, -, *, /, and the modulus operator %. The relational operators are >, >=, <, and <=, which have lower precedence than arithmetic operators. The equality operators are == and !=. Logical operators && (AND) and || (OR) are evaluated left-to-right, and evaluation stops as soon as the truth or falsehood of the result is known (short-circuit evaluation).

1780190881526.title: Chapter 3: Control Flow
1780190881526.content:
Chapter 3: Control Flow

The control-flow statements of a language specify the order in which computations are performed. We have already met the most common control-flow constructions in earlier examples; here we will describe them more completely, and introduce some new ones.

The if-else statement is used to express decisions. Formally, the syntax is:

if (expression)
    statement1
else
    statement2

Where the else part is optional. If the expression evaluates to non-zero (true), statement1 is executed. If it evaluates to zero (false) and there is an else part, statement2 is executed. Because an if simply tests the numeric value of an expression, certain shortcuts are possible. The most obvious is writing if (expression) instead of if (expression != 0).

For multi-way decisions, C provides the else-if chain and the switch statement. The switch statement is a multi-way decision maker that tests whether an expression matches one of a number of constant integer values, and branches accordingly:

switch (expression) {
    case const-expr: statements
    case const-expr: statements
    default: statements
}

C also provides three loop structures: while, for, and do-while. The for loop is equivalent to a while loop but encapsulates the initialization, condition, and increment step in a single line, making the code much more readable:

for (expr1; expr2; expr3)
    statement

Which is equivalent to:

expr1;
while (expr2) {
    statement;
    expr3;
}

1780190881526.title: Chapter 4: Functions and Program Structure
1780190881526.content:
Chapter 4: Functions and Program Structure

Functions break large computing tasks into smaller ones, and enable people to build on what others have done instead of starting over from scratch. Good functions hide details of operation from parts of the program that don't need to know about them, thus clarifying the whole and easing the pain of making changes.

C has been designed to make functions efficient and easy to use. C programs generally consist of many small functions rather than a few big ones. A program may reside in one or more source files, which can be compiled separately and loaded together, along with previously compiled functions from libraries.

Let's look at the basic structure of a function definition:

return-type function-name(parameter-declarations) {
    declarations;
    statements;
}

If the return type is omitted, int is assumed by default. A function returns a value to its caller with the return statement. The return expression is converted to the return type of the function if necessary. If a function does not return a value, its return type should be declared as void.

Communication between functions is done via arguments and external variables. In C, all function arguments are passed "by value". This means that the called function is given local copies of its arguments, not the original variables. Therefore, the called function cannot affect the original variables in the calling function directly. To modify a variable in the caller, the caller must pass the variable's address (a pointer to it), and the called function must declare the parameter as a pointer and access the variable indirectly through it.

1780190881526.title: Chapter 5: Pointers and Arrays
1780190881526.content:
Chapter 5: Pointers and Arrays

A pointer is a variable that contains the address of another variable. Pointers are very much used in C, partly because they are sometimes the only way to express a computation, and partly because they usually lead to more compact and efficient code than can be obtained in other ways. Pointers and arrays are closely related; in this chapter we will also explore this relationship and show how to exploit it.

Let's start with basic pointer notation. If x is an integer, then &x represents the memory address of x. The unary operator & gives the address of an object. The unary operator * is the indirection or dereference operator; when applied to a pointer, it accesses the object the pointer points to.

Here is a simple example showing pointer declarations and assignments:

int x = 1, y = 2, z[10];
int *ip;          /* ip is a pointer to int */

ip = &x;          /* ip now points to x */
y = *ip;          /* y is now 1 */
*ip = 0;          /* x is now 0 */
ip = &z[0];       /* ip now points to z[0] */

The declaration int *ip; is intended as a mnemonic; it says that the expression *ip is an int. The syntax of declarations for variables mimics the syntax of expressions in which the variables might occur.

There is a strong connection between pointers and arrays. Any operation that can be achieved by array subscripting can also be done with pointers. The pointer version will generally be faster but, at least to the uninitiated, somewhat harder to understand. The declaration int a[10]; defines an array of size 10, that is, a block of 10 consecutive objects named a[0], a[1], ..., a[9]. The notation a by itself refers to the address of the zeroth element, i.e., &a[0]. Thus, if pa is a pointer to an integer, the assignment pa = a; sets pa to point to the beginning of the array.

1780193505219.title: Bab 5: Tata Bahasa Dasar & Partikel (Grammar & Particles)
1780193505219.content:
Bab 5: Tata Bahasa Dasar & Partikel (Grammar & Particles)

Partikel (Joshi) adalah elemen terpenting dalam tata bahasa Jepang. Partikel berfungsi sebagai penanda hubungan antar kata di dalam kalimat. Tanpa partikel yang tepat, arti kalimat bisa berubah total atau tidak dapat dipahami sama sekali.

Berikut adalah partikel dasar yang wajib dikuasai oleh pemula:

  • は (wa): Penanda topik utama kalimat. Contoh: 私は学生です (Watashi wa gakusei desu - Saya adalah siswa).
  • が (ga): Penanda subjek fokus, sering digunakan dengan kata kerja intransitif atau kata sifat yang menyatakan keinginan/kemampuan. Contoh: 猫が好きです (Neko ga suki desu - Saya suka kucing).
  • を (o / wo): Penanda objek langsung. Contoh: ご飯を食べます (Gohan o tabemasu - Makan nasi).
  • に (ni): Menandakan waktu spesifik, tempat keberadaan benda, atau objek penerima aksi. Contoh: 七時に起きます (Shichiji ni okimasu - Bangun pada jam 7).
  • で (de): Menandakan tempat terjadinya aktivitas atau alat/metode yang digunakan. Contoh: 図書館で勉強します (Toshokan de benkyou shimasu - Belajar di perpustakaan).
  • の (no): Menandakan kepemilikan atau modifikasi kata benda. Contoh: これは私の車です (Kore wa watashi no kuruma desu - Ini mobil saya).

Mari latihan menyusun kalimat lengkap: subjek + partikel wa + objek + partikel o + kata kerja + desu/masu. Latihlah sesering mungkin untuk membiasakan pola pikir tata bahasa Jepang.

1780192265680.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Antenna Parameters
1780192265680.content:
Chapter 1: Introduction to Antenna Parameters

An antenna is a device that provides a transition between radiation in space and guided waves in transmission lines. In antenna theory, we define several critical parameters to describe how efficiently an antenna transmits or receives electromagnetic radiation. These parameters include radiation patterns, gain, directivity, beamwidth, and impedance matching.

The radiation pattern is a graphical representation of the radiation properties of the antenna as a function of space coordinates. Usually, we plot the radiation pattern in the far-field region, where the angular distribution of radiation is independent of the distance from the antenna. Let the radiation intensity be $U(\theta, \phi)$; the total radiated power $P_{rad}$ is given by integrating the radiation intensity over a sphere:

P_rad = \iint_\Omega U(\theta, \phi) d\Omega = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\pi U(\theta, \phi) \sin\theta d\theta d\phi

Directivity $D$ is the ratio of the radiation intensity in a given direction from the antenna to the radiation intensity averaged over all directions. The average radiation intensity is equal to the total power radiated by the antenna divided by $4\pi$. Mathematically, directivity is expressed as:

D(\theta, \phi) = \frac{4\pi U(\theta, \phi)}{P_rad}

Antenna Gain $G$ is closely related to directivity, but it accounts for the losses of the antenna as well. It is defined as the ratio of the radiation intensity in a given direction to the radiation intensity that would be obtained if the power accepted by the antenna were radiated isotropically. The relationship between gain and directivity is given by $G = \eta_{cd} D$, where $\eta_{cd}$ is the radiation efficiency of the antenna.

1780192265680.title: Chapter 2: Radiation Integrals and Potential Functions
1780192265680.content:
Chapter 2: Radiation Integrals and Auxiliary Potential Functions

In electromagnetics, calculating the radiation field directly from the electric current density $\mathbf{J}$ and magnetic current density $\mathbf{M}$ is complex because the fields are coupled through Maxwell's equations. To simplify this, we introduce auxiliary potential functions. The most common vector potential functions are $\mathbf{A}$ (magnetic vector potential) and $\mathbf{F}$ (electric vector potential).

The vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ is related to the magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ and current density $\mathbf{J}$ through the Helmholtz vector wave equation. In a homogeneous medium, the solution for the vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ at a distance $r$ from the source currents is given by the free-space Green's function integral:

A(x,y,z) = \frac{\mu}{4\pi} \iiint_V J(x',y',z') \frac{e^{-j k R}}{R} dV'

Where $R = \sqrt{(x-x')^2 + (y-y')^2 + (z-z')^2}$ is the distance from the source point $(x',y',z')$ to the observation point $(x,y,z)$, and $k = \omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon} = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the wavenumber of the medium.

Once the potential functions $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ are calculated, we can derive the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ using the curl equations. In the far-field region ($R \approx r$), the integrals simplify significantly. We can approximate $R \approx r - r'\cosθ'$ for phase terms, and $R \approx r$ for amplitude terms. This leads to the transverse electromagnetic (TEM) wave approximations, where the electric and magnetic fields are orthogonal to the direction of propagation.

1780192265680.title: Chapter 3: Linear Wire Antennas
1780192265680.content:
Chapter 3: Linear Wire Antennas

Linear wire antennas are the oldest, simplest, cheapest, and most versatile antennas in practical applications. The dipole antenna, which consists of two straight wires collinear with each other, is the fundamental linear antenna. In this chapter, we evaluate the radiation fields, radiation resistance, directivity, and input impedance of dipoles of various lengths.

Let's consider an infinitesimal dipole of length $dl$ (where $dl \ll \lambda$) aligned along the z-axis and carrying a uniform current $I_0$. The magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ has only a z-component and simplifies to a spherical wave. The resulting far-field components of the electric and magnetic fields are:

E_theta = j \eta \frac{k I_0 dl \sin\theta}{4\pi r} e^{-j k r}

H_phi = j \frac{k I_0 dl \sin\theta}{4\pi r} e^{-j k r}

Where $\eta = \sqrt{\mu/\epsilon} \approx 120\pi \approx 377 \ Ω$ is the intrinsic impedance of free space. Notice that the fields are maximum in the broadside direction ($\theta = 90^\circ$) and zero along the axis of the wire ($\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$).

For a finite-length dipole of length $L$, the current distribution is no longer uniform. It can be modeled as a sinusoidal standing wave along the wire. Integrating the infinitesimal dipole formula over the length $L$ yields the radiation pattern factor. For the half-wavelength dipole ($L = \lambda/2$), the total radiated power is approximately $P_{rad} \approx 36.56 I_0^2$, which corresponds to a radiation resistance $R_{rad} = 2 P_{rad}/I_0^2 \approx 73 \ \u03a9$. This impedance value matches standard coaxial transmission lines, making the half-wave dipole extremely popular.

1780192265680.title: Chapter 4: Loop Antennas
1780192265680.content:
Chapter 4: Loop Antennas

Loop antennas are another basic configuration of antennas that find widespread applications in communication systems, direction-finding, and RFID. Loop antennas can take various shapes, such as circular, rectangular, triangular, or square, but the circular loop is the most common and easiest to analyze mathematically.

Loop antennas are classified into two categories based on their circumference size relative to the wavelength:

  • Small Loops: Circumference is less than one-tenth of a wavelength ($C < 0.1\lambda$). The current distribution is assumed to be uniform in phase and amplitude.
  • Large Loops: Circumference is comparable to the wavelength ($C \approx \lambda$). The current distribution varies sinusoidally and behaves as a standing wave.

An interesting theoretical property of small loop antennas is their equivalence to infinitesimal electric dipoles. A small loop antenna carrying a uniform current $I_0$ generates far-field radiation patterns identical to a magnetic dipole. The radiation resistance of a small loop of radius $a$ and area $A = \pi a^2$ is extremely low:

R_rad = 31200 \left(\frac{A}{\lambda^2}\right)^2

Due to this very low radiation resistance, small loops are very inefficient transmitters. However, they make excellent, compact, low-noise receiving antennas (such as AM radio antennas and NFC antennas) because they respond primarily to the magnetic field rather than electric noise.

1780192265680.title: Chapter 5: Aperture Antennas
1780192265680.content:
Chapter 5: Aperture Antennas

Aperture antennas are antennas that emit electromagnetic waves through an opening or aperture. They are widely used at microwave and millimeter-wave frequencies, where waveguides and horn structures are common. Examples of aperture antennas include rectangular waveguides, horn antennas (sectoral, pyramidal, conical), and reflector antennas (like satellite dishes).

The analysis of aperture antennas relies on the equivalence principle. The field radiated by an aperture can be calculated by replacing the actual source currents behind the aperture with equivalent electric and magnetic currents flowing on a closed surface enclosing the aperture. The equivalent source densities are:

J_s = \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{H}_a

M_s = -\mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{E}_a

Where $\mathbf{E}_a$ and $\mathbf{H}_a$ are the electric and magnetic fields inside the aperture, and $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit normal vector pointing outward.

For a rectangular aperture with uniform field distribution, the radiation pattern can be expressed as a product of sinc functions, similar to the optical diffraction pattern of a slit. The beamwidth and gain of the aperture antenna are directly proportional to the physical dimensions of the aperture opening relative to the wavelength. Horn antennas increase the aperture size gradually to match the wave impedance of the waveguide to free space, minimizing reflections and maximizing directional gain.

1.title: Chapter 1: The Surprising Power of Atomic Habits
1.content:
Chapter 1: The Surprising Power of Atomic Habits

It is so easy to overestimate the importance of one defining moment and underestimate the value of making small improvements on a daily basis. Too often, we convince ourselves that massive success requires massive action. Whether it is losing weight, building a business, writing a book, winning a championship, or achieving any other goal, we put pressure on ourselves to make some earth-shattering improvement that everyone will talk about.

Meanwhile, improving by 1 percent isn't particularly notable—sometimes it isn't even noticeable—but it can be far more meaningful, especially in the long run. The difference this tiny improvement can make over time is astounding. Here is how the math works out: if you can get 1 percent better each day for one year, you’ll end up thirty-seven times better by the time you’re done. Conversely, if you get 1 percent worse each day for one year, you’ll decline nearly down to zero. What starts as a small win or a minor setback accumulates into something much more.

Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. The same way that money multiplies through compound interest, the effects of your habits multiply as you repeat them. They seem to make little difference on any given day, and yet the impact they deliver over the months and years can be enormous. It is only when looking back two, five, or perhaps ten years later that the value of good habits and the cost of bad ones becomes strikingly apparent.

1.title: Chapter 2: How Your Habits Shape Your Identity (And Vice Versa)
1.content:
Chapter 2: How Your Habits Shape Your Identity (And Vice Versa)

Why is it so easy to repeat bad habits and so hard to form good ones? Few things can have a more powerful impact on your life than improving your daily habits. And yet, it is highly likely that this time next year you’ll be doing the same thing rather than something better. It often feels like we are fighting ourselves to make changes. The real reason is that we try to change the wrong thing, or we try to change our habits in the wrong way.

There are three layers of behavior change: a change in your outcomes, a change in your processes, or a change in your identity.

  • Outcomes: This level is concerned with changing your results: losing weight, publishing a book, winning a championship. Most of the goals you set are associated with this level.
  • Processes: This level is concerned with changing your habits and systems: implementing a new routine at the gym, decluttering your desk for better workflow, developing a meditation practice. Most of the habits you build are associated with this level.
  • Identity: This level is concerned with changing your beliefs: your worldview, your self-image, your judgments about yourself and others. Most of the beliefs you hold are associated with this level.

Many people begin the process of changing their habits by focusing on what they want to achieve. This leads us to outcome-based habits. The alternative is to build identity-based habits. With this approach, we start by focusing on who we wish to become. When your habits align with your identity, behavior change becomes natural because you are simply acting in alignment with who you believe you are.
